paragraphs: “For my part, I wish this fine, gifted young man every success. I hope his youthful idealism and his pull toward the ideas of the people never degenerate, as so often happens, into gloomy mysticism on the moral side and blind chauvinism on the political. Those two are an even greater danger to Russia than the premature decay his elder brother is suffering from, the result of misunderstanding European ideas and adopting them for nothing.”

Two or three people clapped at the mention of chauvinism and mysticism. Ippolit Kirillovitch had indeed been carried away by his own eloquence. All this had little to do with the case, and it was rather vague besides, but the sickly, consumptive man was overcome by a longing to speak his mind once in his life. People said afterwards that he had unworthy motives for his criticism of Ivan: Ivan had once or twice got the better of him in argument, and Ippolit Kirillovitch, remembering it, was now trying to take his revenge. I don’t know whether that was true. In any case, all this was only the introduction, and the speech now moved on to the case itself.

“But let us return to the eldest son,” Ippolit Kirillovitch went on. “He is the prisoner before us. We have his life and his actions before us as well. The fatal day has come, and everything has been brought to the surface. His brothers seem to stand for ‘Europeanism’ and ‘the principles of the people.’ He seems to stand for Russia as she is. Oh, not all of Russia, not all! God preserve us if it were! Yet here we have her, our mother Russia, the very scent and sound of her. Oh, he is spontaneous. He is a marvelous mixture of good and evil. He loves culture and Schiller, yet he brawls in taverns and pulls out the beards of his drinking companions. Oh, he, too, can be good and noble, but only when all goes well with him. What is more, he can be swept off his feet, positively swept off his feet, by noble ideals, but only if they come to him of themselves, if they fall from heaven for him, if he does not have to pay for them. He dislikes paying for anything, but he is very fond of receiving, and that is how he is in everything. Oh, give him every possible good in life (he could not be content with less), put no obstacle in his way, and he will show that he, too, can be noble. He is not greedy, no. But he must have money, a great deal of money, and you will see how generously, with what scorn for filthy lucre, he will throw it all away in one night of reckless dissipation. But if he has no money, he will show what he is ready to do to get it when he needs it badly. But all that comes later. Let us take events in the order they happened.

“First, we have before us a poor abandoned child, running about the back yard ‘without boots on his feet,’ as our worthy and esteemed fellow citizen, of foreign origin, alas! put it just now. I say it again: I yield to no one in defending the criminal. I am here to accuse him, but to defend him also. Yes, I, too, am human. I, too, can weigh the influence of home and childhood on a character. But the boy grows up and becomes an officer. For a duel and other reckless conduct he is exiled to one of the remote frontier towns of Russia. There, as an officer, he led a wild life. And of course he needed money, money before all things. So after long disputes he came to a settlement with his father, and the last six thousand was sent to him. A letter exists in which he all but gives up his claim to the rest, and ends his conflict with his father over the inheritance in return for this six thousand.

“Then came his meeting with a young girl of lofty character and brilliant education. Oh, I do not venture to repeat the details; you have only just heard them. Honor and self-sacrifice were shown there, and I will be silent. The figure of the young officer, frivolous and dissolute, paying homage to true nobility and a lofty ideal, appeared to us in a very sympathetic light. But the other side of the coin was turned toward us unexpectedly, right afterwards, in this very court. Again I will not venture to guess why it happened so, but there were causes. The same lady, in tears of long-hidden indignation, declared that he, he of all men, had despised her for what she did. It was an imprudent act, reckless perhaps, but still prompted by lofty and generous motives. He, the girl’s betrothed, looked at her with that mocking smile, which was more unbearable from him than from anyone. And knowing that he had already deceived her (he had deceived her, believing that she was bound to endure everything from him, even betrayal), she deliberately offered him three thousand roubles. She let him understand clearly, too clearly, that she was offering him the money to deceive her. ‘Well, will you take it or not? Are you so lost to shame?’ was the silent question in her searching eyes. He looked at her and saw plainly what was in her mind (he has admitted before you that he understood it all). He took that three thousand without any conditions and squandered it in two days with his new love.

“What are we to believe, then? The first legend, of the young officer giving his last farthing in a noble impulse of generosity and paying reverence to virtue? Or this other, revolting picture? As a rule, between two extremes one has to find the middle, but in the present case that is not true. The likelihood is that in the first case he was truly noble, and in the second just as truly base. And why? Because he had the broad Karamazov nature (that is just what I am leading up to), capable of holding the most incongruous contradictions together, capable of the greatest heights and the greatest depths. Remember the brilliant remark of a young observer who has seen the Karamazov family at close quarters, Mr. Rakitin: ‘The sense of their own degradation is as essential to those reckless, unbridled natures as the sense of their lofty generosity.’ And that is true. They continually need this unnatural mixture. Two extremes at the same moment, or they are miserable and dissatisfied and their existence is incomplete. They are wide, wide as mother Russia. They take in everything and put up with everything.

“By the way, gentlemen of the jury, we have just touched on that three thousand roubles, and I will venture to run ahead of events a little. Can you imagine that a man like that, receiving that sum in such a way, at the price of such shame, such disgrace, such utter degradation, could have been capable that very day of setting aside half of it? That very day, of sewing it up in a little bag? And that he would have had the strength of character to carry it about with him for a whole month afterwards, in spite of every temptation and his extreme need of it? Neither in drunken debauchery in taverns, nor when he was rushing about the countryside trying to get from God knows whom the money he so badly needed to take the woman he loved out of his father’s reach, did he bring himself to touch that little bag! Surely, if only to avoid handing his mistress over to the rival he was so jealous of, he would have opened that bag and stayed at home to guard her. He would have waited for the moment when she finally said to him, ‘I am yours,’ and then fled with her, far from their fatal surroundings.

“But no. He did not touch his talisman, and what reason does he give for it? The chief reason, as I have just said, was that when she said, ‘I am yours, take me where you will,’ he might have the means to take her. But that first reason, in the prisoner’s own words, was of little weight beside the second. While I have that money on me, he said, I am a scoundrel, not a thief. For I can always go to my insulted betrothed, lay down half the sum I took dishonestly, and say to her, ‘You see, I have squandered half your money, and shown that I am a weak and immoral man, and, if you like, a scoundrel’ (I use the prisoner’s own words), ‘but though I am a scoundrel, I am not a thief. If I had been a thief, I would not have brought you back this half of the money. I would have taken it, as I did the other half!’ A marvelous explanation! This frantic but weak man, who could not resist accepting the three thousand roubles at the price of such disgrace, suddenly shows the most stoical firmness. He carries about a thousand roubles without daring to touch it. Does that fit at all with the character we have analyzed? No. And I venture to tell you how the real Dmitri Karamazov would have behaved in such circumstances, if he really had brought himself to put the money away.

“At the first temptation, for instance to entertain the woman with whom he had already squandered half the money, he would have unpicked his little bag and taken out some hundred roubles. For why should he have taken back exactly half the money, that is, fifteen hundred roubles? Why not fourteen hundred? He could just as well have said then that he was not a thief, because he was bringing back fourteen hundred roubles. Then another time he would have unpicked it again and taken out another hundred, and then a third, and then a fourth. Before the end of the month he would have taken out the last note but one, feeling that if he took back only a hundred it would do, since a thief would have stolen it all. And then he would have looked at this last note and said to himself, ‘It is really not worth giving back one hundred. Let us spend that, too!’ That is how the real Dmitri Karamazov, as we know him, would have behaved. One cannot imagine anything more at odds with the facts than this legend of the little bag. Nothing could be more inconceivable. But we shall return to that later.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch went over what the trial had brought out about the money dealings between father and son. He argued again and again that the known facts made it utterly impossible to say which of the two was in the wrong. Then he moved on to the medical experts’ testimony about Mitya’s fixed idea that he was owed three thousand.
